passages.text: FLINT, a hard stone, commonly of a black or grey colour, found in irregular lumps or nodules, chiefly in beds of chalk, where they lie in rows parallel to one another.

Its origin is not known. Some suppose that the flints were once soft, and were formed of the chalk itself, turned into stone by a petrifying juice which penetrated it; and shells and sea urchins are often found within them filled with flint.

Flint strikes fire with steel more readily than any other stone, and is for this reason used in the locks of guns; the sparks being small particles of the steel, cut off and melted by the blow, as Dr Hooke observed with the microscope.
Being burnt and ground to powder, it is used in making glass, and in the finer kinds of earthenware.

The common people in many countries believe that the arrow-heads of flint found in the fields, which they call elf-arrows, are shot by fairies at cattle; others hold them to be formed in the clouds by thunder.
But they are more probably the heads of the weapons of ancient nations who had not the use of iron, such as are still used by the savages of America.
Flint is a hard, sedimentary cryptocrystalline form of the mineral quartz, a variety of chert that occurs in chalk or marly limestone.
Flint occurs as nodules and masses in chalk and limestone, often arranged in layers along the bedding.
The exact way flint forms is still not fully understood. It is thought to form when silica, much of it from the remains of sponges, dissolves and is deposited again within the chalk, replacing it.
Fossils, such as sea urchins, are sometimes preserved in flint.
When struck against steel, flint throws off sparks. The sparks are tiny pieces of steel, shaved off and heated by the blow, that burn in the air.
Flint was widely used in the Stone Age to make tools and weapons, such as hand axes, blades and arrowheads, because it breaks with sharp edges.
Flint was used in flintlock guns from the 17th to the 19th century, and calcined flint was added to pottery and glass.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: nodules, chalk, steel, sparks, arrow-heads.
Chert scores well but covers a wider group of rocks.

britannica.quote: found in irregular lumps or nodules, chiefly in beds of chalk

wikipedia.quote: Flint occurs as nodules and masses in chalk and limestone

alignments.label: Origin not known

wikipedia.quote: The exact way flint forms is still not fully understood.

alignments.note: Both texts admit that the origin is not settled. Wikipedia now gives a likely process.

alignments.label: Chalk turned to stone

britannica.quote: formed of the chalk itself, turned into stone by a petrifying juice

wikipedia.quote: silica, much of it from the remains of sponges, dissolves and is deposited again within the chalk, replacing it

alignments.note: Right that flint takes the place of chalk. The petrifying juice is silica in water, much of it from sponges, and the chalk is replaced, not changed into flint.

alignments.label: Sparks are steel

britannica.quote: the sparks being small particles of the steel, cut off and melted by the blow

wikipedia.quote: The sparks are tiny pieces of steel, shaved off and heated by the blow

alignments.note: Same fact in new words. Hooke saw this with his microscope in the 1660s. Wikipedia adds that the pieces burn in the air.

alignments.label: Glass and earthenware

britannica.quote: it is used in making glass, and in the finer kinds of earthenware

wikipedia.quote: calcined flint was added to pottery and glass

alignments.note: Same uses. Calcined flint is flint that was burnt, as the 1778 entry says.

alignments.label: Shot by fairies

britannica.quote: are shot by fairies at cattle

wikipedia.quote: Flint was widely used in the Stone Age to make tools and weapons

alignments.note: The 1778 entry reports this as a belief of the common people. People made the arrow-heads in the Stone Age.

alignments.label: Formed by thunder

britannica.quote: formed in the clouds by thunder

wikipedia.quote: because it breaks with sharp edges

alignments.note: Thunder does not shape stones. People chose flint for tools because it breaks with sharp edges.

alignments.label: Weapons of ancient nations

britannica.quote: the heads of the weapons of ancient nations who had not the use of iron

wikipedia.quote: such as hand axes, blades and arrowheads

alignments.note: The 1778 entry reached the right view by comparison with tools still in use in America. Wikipedia places these tools in the Stone Age.

alignments.label: A form of quartz

wikipedia.quote: cryptocrystalline form of the mineral quartz

alignments.note: New knowledge. The 1778 entry does not say what flint is made of.

suggestedQuestions: What did the 1778 entry say about flint arrow-heads?
Why does flint make sparks with steel?

What did the 1778 entry say about flint.answer: It reports two popular beliefs: fairies shot them at cattle, or thunder formed them in the clouds [B5]. It then calls them the weapons of ancient nations without iron [B6]. Wikipedia agrees with the last view: Stone Age people made flint tools and arrowheads [W6].

Why does flint make sparks with steel?.answer: The 1778 entry says the sparks are particles of steel cut off and melted by the blow [B3]. Wikipedia gives the same explanation: tiny pieces of steel, heated by the blow, burn in the air [W5].

How does flint form?.answer: The 1778 entry says the origin is not known and reports a guess: chalk turned to stone by a petrifying juice [B2]. Wikipedia says it is still not fully understood, but silica, much of it from sponges, is deposited in the chalk and replaces it [W3].
